item.title: Braxton Cook @ Blue Llama Jazz Club
item.description:
August 16, 2026 — 6:00 PM
Blue Llama Jazz Club

Sun | Aug 16 Sets 6pm & 8pm $85 Dinner & Show $40 Cover Only RESERVE TABLE About the Artist When the vocalist and multi-instrumentalist Braxton Cook first started working on the album that would become Not Everyone Can Go, his life was going through a number of transitions that he just couldn’t ignore. Last year, Cook spent lots of time on the road – in Europe and Asia, along with two United States tours. “I was just very busy, and trying to juggle that with family, it was a lot to manage,” Cook said. In a moment of self-reflection, he looked back on the past year, noticed a theme emerging, and came to this conclusion: It was OK to let go of things that weren’t serving him any longer. Transitions were natural as he stepped into fatherhood. “It was only pushing me more in that direction of understanding,” he continued. “There’s grief that comes along with having to let certain things go to make time for the things I truly value.” One can hear Cook breaking through on Not Everyone Can Go, a mix of jazz and R&B that feels indebted to similar hybrids of yesteryear. Musically, the album conjures images of bright evening sunshine, when the temperature begins to cool. Not quite Quiet Storm, instead, Not Everyone Can Go dabbles between the margins, which won’t surprise those who’ve followed Cook to this point. Across albums like Somewhere In Between, No Doubt and Who Are You When No One Is Watching?, he’s made a career of blurring the lines between genres, landing on a sound that isn’t one thing, in particular. While that’s made his music tough to pin down, that also makes it all the more intriguing. That you can’t label it just R&B or just jazz lends to the music’s attraction. The making of the album also represents a breakthrough for Cook. It was the most collaborative process of his career where he further integrated into his musical network in Los Angeles. Vocal features include NNAVY (“Weekend”) and Marie Dahlstrom (“All My Life”), and additional producers include Bubele on “Bad,” Austin Brown of Hablot Brown on “We’ve Come So Far”, and bassist Kaveh Ragestar (Kneebody) on “All My Life.” Musically, he and his bandmates would improvise and let the energy flow however it needed. One can hear this free-flow on the album’s instrumental tracks – “Zodiac,” “Kingdom Come,” “My Sun” (featuring Elijah Cook), and “Josh’s Tune.” Lyrically, parts of the album address Cook’s realization that life will get better, that even though it’s challenging right now, “the future is bright,” as he sings on the track “My Everything,” the album’s first single. “It’s about a man who continued to selfishly follow his own dreams at the sake of missing the big picture,” Cook said. “And I’m telling myself, ‘We’re going to work through a rough patch here, but things will turn around.” To emphasize that creative focus, Not Everyone Can Go follows the trek of conflict, from where a romantic relationship is going through challenges to when the couple makes it to the other side. The album soundtracks that journey without placing blame on one person or the other. Rather, Cook assesses his own role in the disconnect, as if doing the necessary self work to show up fully for his significant other. “I put ‘My Everything’ near the beginning to establish the conflict,” he said. “Then we work our way through it. By the time we get to ‘We’ve Come So Far,’ it’s a moment of gratitude and a breath in the record – a pop song that’s like, ‘Wait a second, we’re going to be alright.'”  The album’s second half incorporates love songs about the rediscovery of affection. The track “Bad,” which takes sonic cues from late-’90s R&B, with its slow, body-rolling pace and lush electric keys, finds Cook singing about dating his partner with renewed romance. The same goes for “All My Life.” Here, the singer sounds transfixed, akin to the time when you see your partner again, after the storm has passed and the connection feels fresh once more. These songs speak to the kind of cycle found in most relationships, when the day-to-day gets shaky and serious decisions need to be made. But where some decide to part ways in search of someone new, Cook, through these songs, opts to fight for love. Because the partnership is too genuine and there’s a lot of history at stake. “The last part of the album is the action for me,” Cook said. “It’s the act of rebuilding these relationships the way that I want and the way that I see them, and that’s what those love songs are about. ‘Bad’ is very much about taking my wife back out on a date. As if we were just courting each other all over again.” Ultimately, though, Not Everyone Can Go is about embracing change, that when seasons arrive where moves are inevitable, you have to lean into them. RESERVE TABLE

Anchored by fiery mezzo-soprano vocals and wrapped in jazzy R&B textures, her music explores love, intuition, and feminine power with both tenderness and authority. Each song reflects her evolution-not just as an artist, but as a woman deeply attuned to her inner world. Commanding and magnetic on stage, Isis transforms performance into ritual. Inspired by the legacy and modernity of artists such as Tina Turner, Chaka Khan, Prince, she creates music that invites women to untame their inner spirit animals, trust their instincts, and redefine femininity on their own terms. Her presence is immersive, her delivery fearless, and her artistry unmistakably her own. Raised by musicians, Isis has been singing since childhood, with her professional journey beginning in 2012 at Detroit’s legendary Baker’s Keyboard Lounge. Since then, she has shared stages with acclaimed artists including Macy Gray, Darren Criss, Raheem DeVaughn, Brian McKnight, J. Moss, Don Was, and Dave McMurray. Her performances span iconic venues and festivals such as the Detroit Jazz Festival, Concert of Colors, Arts, Beats & Eats, African World Festival, the Detroit Institute of Arts, Motor City Sound Board, Masonic Temple, Cliff Bell’s, and the 50th International African Arts Festival in Brooklyn, NY. Beyond the stage, Isis’s artistry extends into screen and storytelling. She was featured in a national 2020 Ford Escape commercial, as well as WDIV Local 4’s Go 4 It campaign, where she was named a 2023 competition winner. In 2021, she starred as the lead actress in The True Meaning of Christmas, a musical stage play written by Christopher Laird, and earned 3rd place in AMPLIFY: The Sound of Detroit. A graduate of the University of Detroit Mercy with a Bachelor’s degree in Communications, Isis Damil is also an instrumentalist, host, and actress-an artist whose work is rooted in intention, legacy, and the courage to be fully seen. item.description:
September 13, 2026 — 6:00 PM
Blue Llama Jazz Club

Sun | Sep 13 Sets 6pm & 7:30pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist About Pandit Samar Saha Pandit Samar Saha is a titan of the Tabla-the intricate, virtuosic hand drums that form the rhythmic heartbeat of Hindustani classical music. A master of time and nuance, Saha commands a rhythmic vocabulary that rivals the most sophisticated modern percussionists. Hailing from the historic musical center of Kolkata, his playing is defined by a lightning-fast precision and an uncanny ability to engage in complex rhythmic dialogues with his fellow musicians. Whether serving as a sensitive accompanist or a commanding soloist, Saha’s performance is a display of pure technical brilliance and rhythmic invention that captivates listeners of any genre. About Pandit Partha Bose A leading light of the Maihar Gharana, Pandit Partha Bose is a master Sitarist whose artistry bridges ancient tradition and modern expression. To understand Bose is to appreciate the “jazz” of India-his performances are masterclasses in raga (melodic framework) and improvisation, built on a foundation of rigorous technical discipline. Trained under the legacy of Ustad Allauddin Khan, Bose is renowned for his ability to weave complex, meditative tapestries of sound that resonate with deep emotional intelligence. A veteran of the world’s most prestigious stages, he offers an experience that is as intellectually demanding as it is profoundly soulful. Intersection of Hindustani Classical Music and Jazz Hindustani classical music is a meditative, improvisational tradition that has long shared a deep, soulful resonance with Western jazz. For decades, this exchange has captivated audiences, built on a common language of spontaneous creation, intricate rhythmic structures, and a quest for spiritual depth. This cross-cultural fascination became a defining movement in the 1960s, famously sparked by the legendary collaboration between Ravi Shankar and John Coltrane. Coltrane saw in Shankar’s raga system a framework for his own explorations into modal jazz and transcendence, directly influencing works like Africa/Brass and his pursuit of “universal” sounds. Simultaneously, the global spotlight on Indian classical music was amplified by The Beatles-most notably George Harrison-who integrated the haunting timbre of the sitar into the pop lexicon, introducing millions of Western listeners to the hypnotic, microtonal beauty of Indian ragas. Today, this dialogue remains vibrant, as modern jazz masters continue to draw from the Hindustani well of rhythmic complexity and melodic fluidity. When Pandit Partha Bose and Pandit Samar Saha take the stage, they are not merely performing an ancient tradition; they are continuing a storied, high-level musical conversation-one that invites the jazz-savvy listener to lose themselves in the same sense of wonder that has bridge Eastern tradition and Western innovation for generations.
